CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER · OCTOBER

Calculating with natural numbers

A cinema with 18 rows of 24 seats, 1,000 gummy bears for 7 people, a holiday budget with four items: with large numbers you calculate in columns, place by place. In this chapter you add, subtract, multiply and divide in columns, check with an estimate and the inverse calculation, and calculate more cleverly with the laws of arithmetic and the order of operations.

15 LESSONS4 UNITS4 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • add, subtract and multiply in your head, in steps and in columns
  • divide by a one-digit number in writing, also with a remainder
  • check results with an estimate and with the inverse calculation
  • use the order of operations: brackets first, multiplication and division before addition and subtraction
  • calculate cleverly with the laws of arithmetic and make up number stories yourself
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

Calculate: $7 \times 8$

$7 \times 8 = 56$

Calculate: $63 \div 9$

$63 \div 9 = 7$, because $7 \times 9 = 63$.

Calculate: $250 + 380$

$250 + 300 = 550$, $550 + 80 = 630$

Calculate: $1{,}000 - 1$

$1{,}000 - 1 = 999$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Adding and subtracting

The Kühn family is planning their holiday: flight €1,248, hotel €1,595, hire car €386. How much does it all cost together? In your head that gets difficult. In columns it is safe: place under place, from right to left.

When you add, the numbers are called addends and the result is called the sum. When you subtract, you calculate the minuend minus the subtrahend, and the result is called the difference.

Small calculations you do in your head or in steps: $348 + 275 = 348 + 200 + 70 + 5 = 623$. With large numbers you calculate in columns. If a column makes 10 or more, you get a carry for the next column.

Before you calculate, an estimate with rounded numbers helps: is the result close to it? Afterwards you check with the inverse calculation.

KEY POINT · ADDING AND SUBTRACTING IN COLUMNS

addend + addend = sum  ·  minuend − subtrahend = difference

Write the numbers one below the other, place under place: ones under ones, tens under tens. Calculate from right to left. If a column makes 10 or more, you write down the ones and carry the tens to the next column.

Checking: estimate $4{,}700 - 1{,}300 = 3{,}400$ and check $3{,}442 + 1{,}296 = 4{,}738$ for $4{,}738 - 1{,}296 = 3{,}442$.

Two ways of subtracting: when you add on, you ask “from 6 to 8?”; when you exchange, you swap 1 ten for 10 ones. Use the way you know from primary school.

More than two addends: write them all one below the other and add each column completely.

INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING IN COLUMNS

Enter two numbers and reveal the calculation step by step. When you subtract, you can choose between adding on and exchanging.

The holiday costs €3,229. Estimate: $1{,}200 + 1{,}600 + 400 = 3{,}200$.

EXAMPLE 2 · SUBTRACTING WITH A CHECK

Work out $5{,}003 - 2{,}467$ and check your answer.

Estimate: $5{,}000 - 2{,}500 = 2{,}500$.

In columns: ones “from 7 to 13 is 6”, carry 1; tens “from 7 to 10 is 3”, carry 1; hundreds “from 5 to 10 is 5”, carry 1; thousands “from 3 to 5 is 2”.

$5{,}003 - 2{,}467 = 2{,}536$. Check: $2{,}536 + 2{,}467 = 5{,}003$.

Start at the back: $6 + 9 = 15$. Which digit must then be in the tens column if a 2 is to come out there?

Ones: $6 + 9 = 15$, carry 1. Tens: $7 + 4 + 1 = 12$, carry 1. Hundreds: $7 + 5 + 1 = 13$, carry 1. Thousands: $4 + 2 + 1 = 7$. So $4{,}776 + 2{,}549 = 7{,}325$.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Multiplying

A cinema has 18 rows with 24 seats each. How many seats is that? In steps: $18 \times 20 + 18 \times 4 = 360 + 72 = 432$. In columns it is quicker, above all with large numbers.

When you multiply, the numbers are called factors and the result is called the product. Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1,000 is easy: you add one, two or three zeros at the end. $37 \times 100 = 3{,}700$.

In columns you multiply the first factor by each digit of the second factor in turn. Each partial product moves one place to the right. At the end you add the partial products.

KEY POINT · MULTIPLYING IN COLUMNS

factor × factor = product

Multiply the first factor by each digit of the second factor. The last digit of each partial product goes exactly under the digit you are multiplying by. Then you add the partial products.

$352 \times 23$: partial products $704$ and $1{,}056$, together $8{,}096$. Estimate: $400 \times 20 = 8{,}000$.

Swapping allowed: $4 \times 352 = 352 \times 4$. Put the number with fewer digits at the back, then there are fewer partial products.

Carried digits: for $352 \times 4$ you calculate $4 \times 2 = 8$, $4 \times 5 = 20$ (write 0, carry 2), $4 \times 3 + 2 = 14$.

INTERACTIVE · MULTIPLYING IN COLUMNS

Change the factors and watch how the partial products come about and where they move to.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE CINEMA

Work out $18 \times 24$ in columns.

18×24
36
72
432

$18 \times 2 = 36$, the 6 goes under the 2. $18 \times 4 = 72$, the 2 goes under the 4. Then $360 + 72 = 432$.

The cinema has 432 seats.

EXAMPLE 4 · ARE THERE ENOUGH BUSES?

A bus has 52 seats. Are 7 buses enough for 375 people?

$52 \times 7 = 364$. That is fewer than 375.

7 buses are not enough. With 8 buses there are $52 \times 8 = 416$ seats.

The cinema with 432 seats is sold out. A ticket costs €9. How much money does the cinema take?

$432 \times 9 = 3{,}888$. The cinema takes €3,888.

Tom calculates $307 \times 46 = 3{,}070$. Make an estimate and find Tom’s mistake.

Estimate: $300 \times 50 = 15{,}000$. Tom’s result is far too small. He did not move the partial product $307 \times 4 = 1{,}228$ to the left. Correct: $12{,}280 + 1{,}842 = 14{,}122$.

Put the digits 3, 4 and 5 into ☐☐ × ☐ so that the product is as big as possible. And when is it as small as possible?

There are only six possibilities. Try them all.

$53 \times 4 = 212$, $54 \times 3 = 162$, $43 \times 5 = 215$, $45 \times 3 = 135$, $34 \times 5 = 170$, $35 \times 4 = 140$. The biggest is $43 \times 5 = 215$, the smallest $45 \times 3 = 135$. So the biggest digit does not necessarily belong at the front!

TEST YOURSELF!

Calculate: $48 \times 100$

Add two zeros at the end: 4,800.

Calculate in columns: $637 \times 8$

$8 \times 7 = 56$, write 6, carry 5. $8 \times 3 + 5 = 29$, write 9, carry 2. $8 \times 6 + 2 = 50$. Result 5,096.

Calculate in columns: $125 \times 34$

$125 \times 3 = 375$ and $125 \times 4 = 500$, so $3{,}750 + 500 = 4{,}250$.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Dividing

1,000 gummy bears are shared fairly between 7 people. Each person gets 142, and 6 are left over: $1{,}000 \div 7 = 142$ remainder 6. Because $142 \times 7 = 994$, and 6 are still missing to make 1,000.

When you divide, the first number is called the dividend, the second the divisor and the result the quotient. Dividing is the inverse of multiplying: $63 \div 9 = 7$, because $7 \times 9 = 63$.

In writing you divide from left to right. At each place you ask: how many times does the divisor go into it? What is left over moves on with the next digit. If something is left over at the end, that is the remainder.

KEY POINT · DIVIDING IN WRITING

dividend ÷ divisor = quotient

1. How many times does the divisor go into the first digit (or into the first digits)? Write that number in the result.
2. Multiply and subtract.   3. Bring down the next digit. Repeat until there are no digits left.

Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend, for example $142 \times 7 + 6 = 1{,}000$. You cannot divide by 0.

Do not forget the zero: $812 \div 4 = 203$. If the divisor does not go in, you write a 0 in the result.

By 10, 100, 1,000: cross out zeros at the end: $4{,}500 \div 100 = 45$.

INTERACTIVE · DIVIDING IN WRITING

Divide a number by a number from 1 to 9. Each step shows: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.

$952 \div 7 = 136$. Check: $136 \times 7 = 952$.

EXAMPLE 6 · INTERPRETING THE REMAINDER

A minibus has 8 seats for passengers. How many minibuses do you need for 75 people?

$75 \div 8 = 9$ remainder 3, because $9 \times 8 = 72$. The 3 remaining people need a seat as well.

You need 10 minibuses.

The parents’ association has €1,250 for new books. A book costs €9. How many books can it buy? How much money is left over?

$1{,}250 \div 9 = 138$ remainder 8. It can buy 138 books, and €8 are left over.

Find a three-digit number that leaves the remainder 1 each time you divide it by 2, by 3, by 4 and by 5.

Subtract 1 from the number you are looking for. Which numbers is the result then divisible by?

The number minus 1 must be divisible by 2, 3, 4 and 5. The smallest such number is 60, the next ones are 120, 180, … So $120 + 1 = 121$ fits, but so do 181, 241 and so on.

TEST YOURSELF!

Divide in writing: $3{,}136 \div 7$

$3{,}136 \div 7 = 448$. Check: $448 \times 7 = 3{,}136$.

What is the remainder of $500 \div 9$?

$9 \times 55 = 495$, so $500 \div 9 = 55$ remainder 5.

What is the smallest number of benches with 6 seats each that you need for 100 people?

$100 \div 6 = 16$ remainder 4. For the 4 remaining people you need one more bench: 17.

UNIT 44 LESSONS

4Laws of arithmetic and order of operations

Lea calculates $4 + 3 \times 5$ and gets 35. Tim gets 19. Who is right? In mathematics there is a fixed order: multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. So first $3 \times 5 = 15$, then $4 + 15 = 19$. Tim is right.

A calculation made of numbers and operation signs is called an expression. So that everybody gets the same result for the same expression, there is an order of operations. Whatever is to be calculated first goes in brackets.

The laws of arithmetic help you to calculate cleverly. When you add and multiply, you may swap numbers and group them differently: $25 \times 17 \times 4 = 25 \times 4 \times 17 = 100 \times 17 = 1{,}700$. With the distributive law, $7 \times 98 = 7 \times 100 - 7 \times 2 = 686$ becomes easy.

KEY POINT · ORDER OF OPERATIONS AND LAWS OF ARITHMETIC

1. Whatever is in brackets first.   2. Multiplication and division before addition and subtraction: × and ÷ before + and −.   3. Otherwise from left to right. You may know this order as BIDMAS.

Commutative law: $a + b = b + a$ and $a \times b = b \times a$

Associative law: $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ and $(a \times b) \times c = a \times (b \times c)$

Distributive law: $a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$

Letters for numbers: $a$, $b$ and $c$ stand for any numbers. That way a law holds for all numbers at once.

Not with − and ÷: $10 - 4$ is not $4 - 10$, and $100 - 20 - 30 = 50$, not 90.

INTERACTIVE · WHAT IS CALCULATED FIRST?

Choose an expression or type in your own. Each step shows which rule applies at that moment.

EXAMPLE 7 · STEP BY STEP

Work out $48 \div (2 + 6) - 3 \times 2$.

Brackets first: $2 + 6 = 8$. Then multiplication and division before subtraction: $48 \div 8 = 6$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$. Finally $6 - 6$.

$48 \div (2 + 6) - 3 \times 2 = 6 - 6 = 0$

EXAMPLE 8 · CALCULATING CLEVERLY

Work out cleverly: a) $4 \times 39 \times 25$   b) $17 \times 6 + 17 \times 4$

a) Swap: $4 \times 25 \times 39 = 100 \times 39 = 3{,}900$.   b) Distributive law backwards: $17 \times (6 + 4) = 17 \times 10 = 170$.

a) 3,900   b) 170

a) $(17 + 8) \times 4 = 100$   b) $12 \times 9 - 18 = 90$

Four fours: Write each of the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 with exactly four digits 4, with operation signs and brackets.

You may also write 44. $4 \div 4$ is 1.

For example: $0 = 44 - 44$, $1 = 44 \div 44$, $2 = 4 \div 4 + 4 \div 4$, $3 = (4 + 4 + 4) \div 4$, $4 = 4 + (4 - 4) \times 4$, $5 = (4 \times 4 + 4) \div 4$. There are many other solutions.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Number chain: Start at 48. Add 152, multiply by 5, subtract 250 and divide by 50. Where do you end up?

$48 + 152 = 200$, $200 \times 5 = 1{,}000$, $1{,}000 - 250 = 750$, $750 \div 50 = 15$.

Cake sale: For the school fête 37 cakes are baked, and each one is cut into 12 pieces. A piece costs €1. At the end 9 pieces are left over. Write an expression for the takings and work it out.

$37 \times 12 - 9 = 444 - 9 = 435$. The takings come to €435.

Number story: Make up a story for the expression $4 \times 15 + 3 \times 8$ and work out the expression.

For example: four cinema tickets at €15 each and three popcorns at €8 each cost $60 + 24 = 84$ euros.

Number riddle: Mia thinks of a number. She multiplies it by 6, adds 9 and gets 75. Which number did she think of?

Work backwards: what was there before 9 was added?

Backwards: $75 - 9 = 66$, $66 \div 6 = 11$. Check: $11 \times 6 + 9 = 75$. Mia thought of 11.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Young Gauss

Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777 to 1855) from Brunswick is regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of all time. In 1856 his friend Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen told a famous story about his schooldays: the teacher Büttner set the class a long addition problem, a so-called series. Young Gauss, who had only just joined the arithmetic class, put his slate on the table after a short time, with the correct result.

Sartorius does not say exactly which numbers had to be added. The story is usually told like this: all the numbers from 1 to 100. The trick is a shortcut: you put the numbers together in pairs.

$1 + 100 = 101$,   $2 + 99 = 101$,   $3 + 98 = 101$, …   That makes 50 pairs, so $50 \times 101 = 5{,}050$.

Try it yourself: Use the trick to add all the numbers from 1 to 20. And from 1 to 1,000?

1 to 20: 10 pairs with the sum 21, so $10 \times 21 = 210$. 1 to 1,000: 500 pairs with the sum 1,001, so $500 \times 1{,}001 = 500{,}500$.

Sources: Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen, “Gauß zum Gedächtniss”, Leipzig 1856. Brian Hayes, “Gauss’s Day of Reckoning”, American Scientist 94 (3), 2006: he compared more than a hundred versions of the story.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

ADDING AND SUBTRACTING

addend + addend = sum, minuend − subtrahend = difference; place under place, with carrying

$4{,}738 + 1{,}296 = 6{,}034$; check: $6{,}034 - 1{,}296 = 4{,}738$

MULTIPLYING

factor × factor = product; partial products one below the other, moved along, then added

$352 \times 23 = 7{,}040 + 1{,}056 = 8{,}096$

DIVIDING

dividend ÷ divisor = quotient; divide, multiply, subtract, bring down

$1{,}000 \div 7 = 142$ remainder 6, because $142 \times 7 + 6 = 1{,}000$

ORDER OF OPERATIONS

Brackets first, × and ÷ before + and −, otherwise from left to right

$4 + 3 \times 5 = 19$; $(4 + 3) \times 5 = 35$

SHORTCUTS

Swap, group differently, distribute

$25 \times 17 \times 4 = 1{,}700$; $7 \times 98 = 700 - 14 = 686$
